{{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|ja|津駅|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism Association|ja|津市観光協会|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Public Service Academy|ja|三重公務員学院|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ast Plaza|ja|アストプラザ|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ohara Gakuen|ja|大原学園|12=draft}} * {{ill|Okawa Gakuen|ja|学校法人大川学園 (三重県)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tokai Regional Agricultural Administration Office|ja|東海農政局|12=draft}} Mie Agricultural Office * {{ill|Mie Prefectural Office|ja|三重県庁舎|12=draft}} ** {{ill|Mie Prefectural Assembly|ja|三重県議会|12=draft}} Assembly Hall == Access == * Car: About 5 minutes from Tsu Interchange * JR/Kintetsu/Bus: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Tsu Station == Related Organizations == * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Supporters Association|ja|三重縣護國神社奉賛会|12=draft}} - founded in January 1986 (Showa 61) ** First president: Masao Yamashita (68th Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) ** Second president: Rinpei Nonaka (73rd Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) ** Third president: Kazumi Otobe (87th Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) ** Fourth president: Nobuyuki Nishiba (92nd Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) * {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁|12=draft}} ** First head: Yoshiro Hase ** Second head: Shinsuke Takatsukasa ** Third head: Yukitada Sasaki ** Fourth head: Munetada Tokugawa ** Fifth head: Morisada Hosokawa ** Sixth head: Motofumi Higashisono ** Seventh head: Kuninori Kuni ** Eighth head: Michihisa Kitashirakawa ** Ninth head: Naotake Takatsukasa * {{ill|Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership|ja|神道政治連盟|12=draft}} * {{ill|Nippon Kaigi|ja|日本会議|12=draft}} ** First president: Koichi Tsukamoto ** Second president: Kosaku Inaba ** Third president: Tatsu Miyoshi ** Fourth president: Tadae Takubo * {{ill|Association to Commemorate the Spirits of the War Dead|ja|英霊にこたえる会|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association|ja|三重県遺族会|12=draft}} ** First president: Shinzaburo Aoyama ** Second president: Kirowo Mizutani ** Third president: Yoshizou Kawai ** Fourth president: Goro Fuchida ** Fifth president: Noboru Saito ** Sixth president: Gen Tamura ** Seventh president: Yoshiaki Tani ** Eighth president: Juro Saito ** Ninth president: Norihisa Tamura == Notes == {{Reflist}} Mie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku ShrineMie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku ShrineMie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku ShrineMie Gokoku Shrine}} == External Links == {{Commonscat|Mieken-Gokoku-jinja}} * [https://miegokoku.jimdo.com Official Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Homepage] * {{Facebook|miegokoku}} * {{Instagram|mieken_gokokujinja}} * {{Twitter|miegokoku}} * {{YouTube|c=UCocdnRI2Htda2eWuYA-I3_Q}} * [https://www.kankomie.or.jp/spot/detail_21599.html Mie Tourism Federation - {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|ja|津駅|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism Association|ja|津市観光協会|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Public Service Academy|ja|三重公務員学院|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ast Plaza|ja|アストプラザ|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ohara Gakuen|ja|大原学園|12=draft}} * {{ill|Okawa Gakuen|ja|学校法人大川学園 (三重県)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tokai Regional Agricultural Administration Office|ja|東海農政局|12=draft}} Mie Agricultural Office * {{ill|Mie Prefectural Office|ja|三重県庁舎|12=draft}} ** {{ill|Mie Prefectural Assembly|ja|三重県議会|12=draft}} Assembly Hall == Access == * Car: About 5 minutes from Tsu Interchange * JR/Kintetsu/Bus: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Tsu Station == Related Organizations == * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Supporters Association|ja|三重縣護國神社奉賛会|12=draft}} - {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|ja|津駅|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism Association|ja|津市観光協会|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Public Service Academy|ja|三重公務員学院|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ast Plaza|ja|アストプラザ|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ohara Gakuen|ja|大原学園|12=draft}} * {{ill|Okawa Gakuen|ja|学校法人大川学園 (三重県)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tokai Regional Agricultural Administration Office|ja|東海農政局|12=draft}} Mie Agricultural Office * {{ill|Mie Prefectural Office|ja|三重県庁舎|12=draft}} ** {{ill|Mie Prefectural Assembly|ja|三重県議会|12=draft}} Assembly Hall == Access == * Car: About 5 minutes from Tsu Interchange * JR/Kintetsu/Bus: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Tsu Station == Related Organizations == * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Supporters Association|ja|三重縣護國神社奉賛会|12=draft}} - founded in January 1986 (Showa 61) ** First president: Masao Yamashita (68th Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) ** Second president: Rinpei Nonaka (73rd Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) ** Third president: Kazumi Otobe (87th Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) ** Fourth president: Nobuyuki Nishiba (92nd Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman) * {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁|12=draft}} ** First head: Yoshiro Hase ** Second head: Shinsuke Takatsukasa ** Third head: Yukitada Sasaki ** Fourth head: Munetada Tokugawa ** Fifth head: Morisada Hosokawa ** Sixth head: Motofumi Higashisono ** Seventh head: Kuninori Kuni ** Eighth head: Michihisa Kitashirakawa ** Ninth head: Naotake Takatsukasa * {{ill|Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership|ja|神道政治連盟|12=draft}} * {{ill|Nippon Kaigi|ja|日本会議|12=draft}} ** First president: Koichi Tsukamoto ** Second president: Kosaku Inaba ** Third president: Tatsu Miyoshi ** Fourth president: Tadae Takubo * {{ill|Association to Commemorate the Spirits of the War Dead|ja|英霊にこたえる会|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association|ja|三重県遺族会|12=draft}} ** First president: Shinzaburo Aoyama ** Second president: Kirowo Mizutani ** Third president: Yoshizou Kawai ** Fourth president: Goro Fuchida ** Fifth president: Noboru Saito ** Sixth president: Gen Tamura ** Seventh president: Yoshiaki Tani ** Eighth president: Juro Saito ** Ninth president: Norihisa Tamura == Notes == {{Reflist}} Mie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku ShrineMie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku ShrineMie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku Shrine}} Mie Gokoku ShrineMie Gokoku Shrine}} == External Links == {{Commonscat|Mieken-Gokoku-jinja}} * [https://miegokoku.jimdo.com Official Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Homepage] * {{Facebook|miegokoku}} * {{Instagram|mieken_gokokujinja}} * {{Twitter|miegokoku}} * {{YouTube|c=UCocdnRI2Htda2eWuYA-I3_Q}} * [https://www.kankomie.or.jp/spot/detail_21599.html Mie Tourism Federation - {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=[[File:MIe Gokoku Shrine Haiden.jpg|140405 Mieken-gokoku-jinja Tsu MIe pref Japan02s3|300px]] | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft|12=draft}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{coord|34|43|58|N|136|30|31|E|}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft|12=draft}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=draft|12=draft}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭|12=draft|12=draft}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日|12=draft|12=draft}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=draft|12=draft}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日|12=draft|12=draft}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft|12=draft}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭|12=draft|12=draft}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=draft|12=draft}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|ja|津駅|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism Association|ja|津市観光協会|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Public Service Academy|ja|三重公務員学院|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ast Plaza|ja|アストプラザ|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ohara Gakuen|ja|大原学園|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Okawa Gakuen|ja|学校法人大川学園 (三重県)|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tokai Regional Agricultural Administration Office|ja|東海農政局|12=draft|12=draft}} Mie Agricultural Office * {{ill|Mie Prefectural Office|ja|三重県庁舎|12=draft|12=draft}} ** {{ill|Mie Prefectural Assembly|ja|三重県議会|12=draft|12=draft}} Assembly Hall == Access == * Car: About 5 minutes from Tsu Interchange * JR/Kintetsu/Bus: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Tsu Station == Related Organizations == * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Supporters Association|ja|三重縣護國神社奉賛会|12=draft|12=draft}} - [[October 22]] }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[Shinto shrine|shrine]] ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社|12=draft|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|12=draft|12=draft}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon Incident|ja|禁門の変|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft|12=draft}} to {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft|12=draft}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|ja|靖国神社|1=Yasukuni Shrine|12=draft|12=draft}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year|12=draft|12=draft}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷|12=draft|12=draft}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=draft|12=draft}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社|12=draft|12=draft}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|ja|津駅|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism Association|ja|津市観光協会|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Mie Public Service Academy|ja|三重公務員学院|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ast Plaza|ja|アストプラザ|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ohara Gakuen|ja|大原学園|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Okawa Gakuen|ja|学校法人大川学園 (三重県)|12=draft|12=draft}} * {{ill|Tokai Regional Agricultural Administration Office|ja|東海農政局|12=draft|12=draft}} Mie Agricultural Office * {{ill|Mie Prefectural Office|ja|三重県庁舎|12=draft|12=draft}} ** {{ill|Mie Prefectural Assembly|ja|三重県議会|12=draft|12=draft}} Assembly Hall == Access == * Car: About 5 minutes from Tsu Interchange * JR/Kintetsu/Bus: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Tsu Station == Related Organizations == * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Supporters Association|ja|三重縣護國神社奉賛会|12=draft|12=draft}} - On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|ja|明治2nd year}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|ja|津藩}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|ja|藤堂高猷}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|ja|京都霊山護国神社}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinensai|ja|祈年祭}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分の日}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分の日}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三}} * November 23: {{ill|Niinamesai|ja|新嘗祭}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|ja|津駅}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism Association|ja|津市観光協会}} * {{ill|Mie Public Service Academy|ja|三重公務員学院}} * {{ill|Ast Plaza|ja|アストプラザ}} * {{ill|Ohara Gakuen|ja|大原学園}} * {{ill|Okawa Gakuen|ja|学校法人大川学園 (三重県)}} * {{ill|Tokai Regional Agricultural Administration Office|ja|東海農政局}} Mie Agricultural Office * {{ill|Mie Prefectural Office|ja|三重県庁舎}} ** {{ill|Mie Prefectural Assembly|ja|三重県議会}} Assembly Hall == Access == * Car: About 5 minutes from Tsu Interchange * JR/Kintetsu/Bus: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Tsu Station == Related Organizations == * {{ill|Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine Supporters Association|ja|三重縣護國神社奉賛会}} - '''三重県護国神社'''（みえけんごこくじんじゃ）は、[[三重県]][[津市]]にある[[神社]]（[[護国神社]]）である。[[禁門の変]]・[[戊辰戦争]]から[[第二次世界大戦]]までの三重県関係の戦歿者6万3百余柱を祀る。これらの祭神は靖国神社の祭神と基本的に重なるが、護国神社が独自で招魂したものであるから、[[靖国神社]]とは本社分社の関係にはないとされる。 近年では、三重県の守り神、子供の神様として県内外から篤い崇敬を集めている。社紋は桜紋であり、[[靖国神社]]や護国神社の多くは社紋に桜を用いている。刊行物に『三重護国』があり、現在は春秋の年2回発行されている。創刊は1960年（昭和35年）10月である。創刊号は16頁にも及び、三重県知事[[田中覚]]、三重県議会議長小久保久吉、津市長角永清、三重県町村会長西浦清乃助、[[神社本庁]]統理[[佐佐木行忠|佐々木行忠]]、[[伊勢神宮|神宮]][[大宮司]][[坊城俊良]]、靖国神社[[筑波藤麿]]、三重県遺族会会長斎藤昇ら各界の著名人が寄稿している。 == 歴史　–明治時代– == 三重県護国神社の歴史は[[1869年]]（[[明治]]2年）、第11代[[津藩]]主であった[[藤堂高猷]]が、[[戊辰戦争]]で戦死した藩士の霊を祀る小祠を津八幡宮の境内に建て、「表忠社」と称したのに始まるとされている。これは幕末の[[長州藩]]や[[薩摩藩]]らが国事殉難者、戦没者の御霊を祀るために招魂場を設けて招魂祭を営んでいた事が淵源となっている。幕府のみならず、朝廷においても1868年（慶応4年）5月10日の太政官布告「癸以来唱義精忠国事ニ斃ルヽ者ノ霊魂ヲ慰シ東山ニ祠宇ヲ設ケテ之ヲ合祀セシム」と「東山ニ一社ヲ建テ当春伏見戦争以来戦死者ノ霊魂ヲ祭祀セシム」とにより、1853年（嘉永6年）以来の国事殉難者と伏見戦争以後の戦死者を京都東山に建立した祀宇（霊山官祭招魂社、後の[[京都霊山護国神社]]）に合祀するなど、慰霊に対する気運が高まっていた事が分かる。 1874年（明治7年）3月17日の内務省達乙第22號によっていわゆる官祭となった。内務省達乙第22號の内容は「戊申己巳之際従軍殉國ノ者戦没ノ地及其他各所ニ於テ舊藩主或ハ人民共私設致シ候招魂場ノ儀ハ永ク忠士ノ魂魄ヲ御吊慰被為在候御趣意ヲ以テ自今其所在ノ地税ヲ免シ祭祀幷修繕共一切官費支給可致旨被仰出候ニ付此旨相達候事」であり、招魂場敷地の地租免除と祭祀や修繕にかかる費用には官費を支給すると明記されている。 翌1875年（明治8年）10月13日に出された内務省達乙第132號によって[[招魂社]]となった。内務省達乙第百132號の内容は「各管内ニ設置有之招魂社ノ儀従前其所在ノ地名等種々ノ社號ヲ附シ來候向モ有之候處自今種々ノ社號ハ都テ相廢シ一般招魂社ト相唱候様可致此旨相達候事」とあり、三重県のみならず東京都（当時の東京府）を除く全ての招魂社の名称を統一した。 東京にあった東京招魂社は1879年（明治12年）6月4日の「東京招魂社靖國神社ト改稱別格官幣社内務陸海軍三省管理祭典其他常務取扱區分」によって現在の社名である靖國神社と改称し、[[別格官幣社]]という社格に列せられた。 1886年（明治19年）6月28日に西南戦争戦没者の御霊の合祀祭申請が有志総代から提出された。以下は、その原文である。 {|class="wikitable" |台湾西南両役従軍殉難ノ霊ヲ招魂社ヘ合祀願 伊勢國安濃郡八幡町八幡神社境内ニ鎮祭スル招魂社ノ義ハ舊津藩藤堂家ニ於テ戊辰巳己ノ際摂州山﨑及奥羽ノ役ニ戦死ノ士卒ヲ祀リ 明治八年以来特ニ官祭ニ被列候モノニ有之茲ニ明治八年　王師台湾ニ向フテ罪ヲ問ヒ曁ヒ十年西南ノ賊ヲ討セラルルニ當リ縣下ノ士 民軍ニ従ヒ　王事ニ死スル者三百七拾八人奮テ王の愾ニ敵シ砲弾ヲ冒シ白刃ヲ踏ミ遂ニ其身ヲ致ス其忠勇壮烈縣下人民ノ㝡モ敬愛シ 㝡モ尊重スル所ニ有之候而メ此三百七拾八人ノ者ハ幸ニ靖國神社ニ合祀セラレ優渥ノ祀典ヲ享ルヲ得タリト雖モ縣地ノ東京ヲ距ル百 有餘里其父子親戚及縣下人民盛儀ヲ拝シテ敬愛尊重ノ意ヲ致ス能ハス誠ニ遺憾ノ至ニ御坐候就テハ前述招魂社ノ義ハ去ル十四年十月
