[[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: [[:en:Kinen-sai|Kinensai]] * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * [[:en:Vernal Equinox Day|Vernal Equinox Day]]: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * [[:en:Autumnal Equinox Day|Autumnal Equinox Day]]: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: [[:en:Shichi-Go-San|Shichi-Go-San]] * November 23: [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: [[:en:Kinen-sai|Kinensai]] * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * [[:en:Vernal Equinox Day|Vernal Equinox Day]]: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * [[:en:Autumnal Equinox Day|Autumnal Equinox Day]]: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: [[:en:Shichi-Go-San|Shichi-Go-San]] * November 23: [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kairaku Park|1=Tsu The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. [[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: [[:en:Kinen-sai|Kinensai]] * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * [[:en:Vernal Equinox Day|Vernal Equinox Day]]: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * [[:en:Autumnal Equinox Day|Autumnal Equinox Day]]: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: [[:en:Shichi-Go-San|Shichi-Go-San]] * November 23: [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). [[commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: [[:en:Kinen-sai|Kinensai]] * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * [[:en:Vernal Equinox Day|Vernal Equinox Day]]: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * [[:en:Autumnal Equinox Day|Autumnal Equinox Day]]: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: [[:en:Shichi-Go-San|Shichi-Go-San]] * November 23: [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kairaku Park|1=Tsu [[commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. [[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: [[:en:Kinen-sai|Kinensai]] * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * [[:en:Vernal Equinox Day|Vernal Equinox Day]]: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * [[:en:Autumnal Equinox Day|Autumnal Equinox Day]]: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: [[:en:Shichi-Go-San|Shichi-Go-San]] * November 23: [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). [[co:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[co:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: [[:en:Kinen-sai|Kinensai]] * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * [[:en:Vernal Equinox Day|Vernal Equinox Day]]: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * [[:en:Autumnal Equinox Day|Autumnal Equinox Day]]: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: [[:en:Shichi-Go-San|Shichi-Go-San]] * November 23: [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kairaku Park|1=Tsu [[co:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[co:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the [[:en:Kinmon incident|Kinmon Incident]] and [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]] to [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to [[:en:1869|Meiji 2]], when the 11th lord of [[:en:Tsu Domain|Tsu Domain]], [[:en:Tōdō Takayuki|Tōdō Takayuki]], built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the [[:en:Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine]]. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. [[co:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[co:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] [[sn:commons:Category:Mieken-Gokoku-jinja]][[ja:三重県護国神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11357857]] Wikidata name: Mieken-Gokoku-jinja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:09, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name=Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | image=File:Mie Gokoku Shrine Torii.jpg | location={{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}}, , Hiromachi 387 | coordinates={{Coord|34.73278|N|136.50861|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity=National martyrs | founded=1869 (Meiji 2) | shrine_Rank=Minister of Home Affairs Designated Gokoku Shrine, Beppyo Shrine | annual_festival=[[April 22]]
[[October 22]] | prefecture={{ill|Tsu|WD=Q203027}} }} [[File:三重県護国神社御朱印帳.jpg|thumb|right|Goshuin book adorned with the shrine crest of sakura|110px]] '''Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine''' (三重県護国神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=shrine}} ({{ill|Gokoku shrines|en|Gokoku shrines|WD=Q1534477|lt=Gokoku Shrine}}) located in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}}, . It enshrines over 60,300 war dead from Mie Prefecture, from the {{ill|Kinmon incident|en|Kinmon incident|WD=Q139871|lt=Kinmon Incident}} and {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War}} to {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|WD=Q362|lt=World War II}}. While its enshrined deities overlap with those of the {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}}, it is not considered a branch of Yasukuni Shrine as Gokoku Shrines independently enshrine spirits. In recent years, it has been revered as a guardian deity of Mie Prefecture and a deity for children, attracting devoted worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture. The shrine crest is a sakura, and many Gokoku Shrines, including Yasukuni Shrine, use sakura as their crest. The publication "Mie Gokoku" is issued twice a year in spring and autumn. The first issue was published in October 1960 (Showa 35), featuring contributions from prominent figures including Mie Prefecture Governor Satoru Tanaka, Mie Prefecture Assembly Chairman Hisakichi Kokubo, Tsu Mayor Kiyoshi Kakunaga, Mie Prefecture Town and Village Association Chairman Seinosuke Nishiura, Association of Shinto Shrines Chief Sasaki Yukitada, Ise Grand Shrine Chief Priest Tosuke Bōjō, Yasukuni Shrine Chief Priest Tsukuba Fujimaro, and Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Chairman Saito Noboru. == History – Meiji Era == The history of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to {{ill|1869|en|1869|WD=Q7720|lt=Meiji 2}}, when the 11th lord of {{ill|Tsu Domain|en|Tsu Domain|WD=Q1060551|lt=Tsu Domain}}, {{ill|Tōdō Takayuki|en|Tōdō Takayuki|WD=Q7425575|lt=Tōdō Takayuki}}, built a small shrine in the grounds of {{ill|Tsu Hachimangu|ja|津八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsu Hachimangu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to enshrine the spirits of retainers who died in the Boshin War, calling it the "Hyochu-sha." This was inspired by the establishment of spirit summoning places and spirit summoning festivals by the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains during the late Edo period to honor national martyrs and war dead. Both the shogunate and the imperial court were motivated by the desire to commemorate the spirits of those who had died in service to the nation, as evidenced by the Daijōkan Proclamation of May 10, 1868 (Keiō 4), which called for the establishment of a shrine in Kyoto's Higashiyama to enshrine these spirits. This led to the creation of the {{ill|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|en|Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine|WD=Q3201026|lt=Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine}}. On March 17, 1874 (Meiji 7), an order from the Ministry of Home Affairs designated it as an official shrine. The order stated that the private spirit summoning places established by former domain lords or people for those who had died in the Boshin and other wars would be exempt from land taxes and that the costs of rituals and repairs would be covered by the government. On October 13, 1875 (Meiji 8), another order from the Ministry of Home Affairs unified the names of all spirit summoning shrines nationwide, renaming them "Shokonsha" (招魂社). The Tokyo Shokonsha was renamed Yasukuni Shrine on June 4, 1879 (Meiji 12), and was designated a Bekkaku Kanpeisha (Special Government Shrine). On June 28, 1886 (Meiji 19), an application was submitted by local representatives to enshrine the spirits of those who died in the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion}}. == History – Showa Era and Beyond == On March 15, 1939 (Showa 14), the shrine was renamed from Koshoko Shrine to Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 12. The rituals and offerings were standardized by Ministry of Home Affairs Order No. 13. On April 1, 1939, Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 142 designated Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine as a specified Gokoku Shrine. In 1945 (Showa 20), the shrine buildings, except for the main hall and sacred hall, were destroyed by air raids. After World War II, the shrine was temporarily renamed "Mie Shrine," but it was restored to its original name in 1953 (Showa 28) when Japan regained its sovereignty. In 1982 (Showa 57), reconstruction projects began, including the rebuilding of the main hall and other facilities, completed in 1983 (Showa 58). In 2019 (Reiwa 1), the shrine celebrated its 150th anniversary with various commemorative projects. == Cultural Properties == Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine owns the prefectural tangible cultural property "Sword, Inscription (Front) Nōshū Mikatsuyama-jū Fujiwara Nagasada (Back) Man'en Gannen Kōshin Hachigatsu Kichijitsu Yori Hitoji" measuring 71.0 cm in blade length and 1.7 cm in curvature. The swordsmith Fujiwara Nagasada, born in 1809 (Bunka 6) in Tairamura, Mino Province (now Gifu Prefecture), is known for his Ise craftsmanship. == annual Events and festivals == * January 1: {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}} * January 15: Dondo Yaki * February 11: {{ill|Kigensai|ja|紀元祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kigensai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 紀元節|1=Kigen-setsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11604982}} * February 17: {{ill|Kinen-sai|en|Kinen-sai|WD=Q118906710|lt=Kinensai}} * February 23: Tenchosai * March 3: Ohina Matsuri * {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|en|Vernal Equinox Day|WD=Q1049141|lt=Vernal Equinox Day}}: Shunbun festival * April 22: Spring Grand festival * April 29: Showa festival * May 5: Children's Warrior Visit * June 30: {{ill|Nagoshi no Harae|ja|夏越大祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoshi no Harae|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓|1=ōharae|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261910}} * August 13: Mantou Mitama festival Lighting ceremony * August 14: Shinen Mitama festival * August 15: Mantou Mitama festival * August 15: Spirit Thanksgiving festival * {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|en|Autumnal Equinox Day|WD=Q1186410|lt=Autumnal Equinox Day}}: Shubun festival * October 22: Autumn Grand festival * November 3: Meiji festival * November 15: {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|en|Shichi-Go-San|WD=Q1072387|lt=Shichi-Go-San}} * November 23: {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en|Niiname-no-Matsuri|WD=Q11501518|lt=Niinamesai}} * December 31: Year-End Purification ceremony and New Year's Eve festival * Monthly: {{ill|Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|ja|月次祭|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukinami-no-Matsuri|qq=}} (1st and 15th) * Memorial services for deities held as needed == Lion Dogs and Stone Lanterns == *'''Aa no Komainu''' - Unusually, both lion dogs at Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine have their mouths open ("aa" pose). It is speculated that originally there were two pairs, with one pair in the "aa" and the other in the "un" pose, but the "un" pair was lost during the war. *'''Aun no Komainu''' - The pair of lion dogs with one mouth open ("aa") and one closed ("un") was dedicated in 1909 (Meiji 42) by members of the Mie Prefecture Assembly. *'''Stone Lanterns''' - Six stone lanterns were dedicated in October 1983 (Showa 58), each inscribed with a poem from the Manyoshu collection by Chief Priest Ujitoko. == Stone Torii and Memorials == *'''Shagō-hi''' - A stone torii gate dedicated in October 1957 (Showa 32) by the Banko Ceramics Cooperative Association. *'''Hy akudo-ishi''' - A stone for the 100 prayers ritual dedicated by 100 people, including Yoshio Hirowo, in a blessed year of Showa 58. *'''Imperial Visit Commemorative Monument''' - Commemorating the visit of Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun on October 27, 1975 (Showa 50). *'''Mother's Statue''' - Dedicated by the children who lost their fathers during the war, honoring their mothers for their hardships and praying for world peace, erected in December 1975 (Showa 50). *'''War Dead Memorial Monument''' - Listing the numbers of military and civilian deaths by major battle areas during the Great East Asia War, dedicated in May 1995 (Heisei 7) by the Mie Prefecture Bereaved Families Association Youth Division. *'''151st Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 151st Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''133rd Infantry Regiment Memorial Monument''' - Memorializing the fallen of the 133rd Infantry Regiment, dedicated in April 1957 (Showa 32) by surviving members. *'''1st Guards Regiment Monument''' - Dedicated in April 2009 (Heisei 21) by the Mie Prefecture 1st Guards Association. == Relationship with Ise Jingu == File:Mie-ken gokoku jinja torii.jpg|The grand torii of Mie Prefecture Gokoku Shrine File:三重県護国神社に参拝される神宮祭主.jpg|The visit of Jingu Saishu Atsuko Ikeda File:三重県護国神社扁額.jpg|Shrine name plaque inscribed by the Jingu Saishu == Surroundings == * {{ill|Kairaku Park|ja|偕楽公園|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kairaku Park|1=Tsu Kairaku Park|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11387140}} * {{ill|Tsu Station|en|Tsu Station|WD=Q869763|lt=Tsu Station}} * {{ill|Tsu City Tourism
